questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the head of a singly linked list, given the head pointer?

options.text: O(n)
O(log n)

questions.explanation: Point the new node's next at the current head and move the head pointer to the new node, two constant-time operations, independent of list length.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of accessing the k-th element of a singly linked list?

options.text: O(log n)
O(n log n)
O(k)

questions.explanation: There is no index arithmetic; you must follow next pointers from the head k times. This lack of random access is the linked list's main disadvantage against an array.

questions.prompt: What does a doubly linked list store in each node that a singly linked list does not?

options.text: A copy of the head pointer
The length of the list
A pointer to the previous node
A pointer to the tail

questions.explanation: The extra previous pointer allows backward traversal and O(1) deletion of a node given only that node. The cost is more memory per node and more pointers to maintain on every update.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm detects a cycle in a linked list using O(1) extra space?

options.text: Floyd's tortoise and hare (two pointers at different speeds)
Storing every visited node in a hash set
Sorting the nodes by address
Reversing the list twice

questions.explanation: A slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two will meet inside a cycle, and never meet if the list ends. The hash-set method also works but costs O(n) space.

questions.prompt: How do you find the middle node of a singly linked list in a single pass?

options.text: Advance a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps until the fast one reaches the end
Count all nodes, then traverse to n/2
Reverse the list and take the head
Use binary search on the node indices

questions.explanation: When the fast pointer reaches the end after moving twice as fast, the slow pointer sits at the midpoint. Counting first also works but needs two passes; binary search is impossible without random access.

questions.prompt: How can a singly linked list be reversed iteratively using O(1) extra space?

options.text: Recurse to the end and rebuild; this uses O(n) stack
Walk the list re-pointing each node's next to its predecessor, tracking previous and current
Swap the head and tail pointers
Copy all values into an array and reverse it

questions.explanation: Keeping previous, current and a saved next, you flip each link as you advance. The array copy and the recursive method both use O(n) extra space.

questions.prompt: A circular linked list is a natural fit for implementing which structure?

options.text: A round-robin queue or buffer that wraps around
A min-heap
A binary search tree
A hash table

questions.explanation: Because the tail links back to the head, traversal naturally cycles, which suits round-robin scheduling and ring buffers. Reaching any node lets you reach all others.

questions.prompt: Compared with an array holding the same values, a linked list has which drawback?

options.text: It cannot store duplicate values
It cannot grow beyond a fixed size
Insertion at a known position is slower
Extra memory per element for pointers and poor cache locality

questions.explanation: Each node stores at least one pointer besides its data, and nodes scattered across memory defeat the CPU cache. Arrays store values contiguously, which is far friendlier to the cache.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of merging two sorted linked lists of sizes m and n into one sorted list?

options.text: O(log(m + n))
O(m x n)
O(m + n)
O((m + n) log (m + n))

questions.explanation: Walk both lists once, at each step splicing the smaller head onto the result. Every node is visited exactly once, giving linear time with O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: To delete a node from a singly linked list given only a pointer to that node (not the head, and it is not the tail), a common trick is to:

options.text: Set this node's pointer to null
It is impossible under any circumstances
Traverse from the head to find the previous node
Copy the next node's value into this node, then delete the next node

questions.explanation: You cannot reach the predecessor, but overwriting this node with its successor's data and then unlinking the successor achieves the same effect in O(1). It fails only for the tail node, which has no successor to copy.
